title: The preacher (Kern ch. 10)
hookLine: whoever keeps even one verse of this sutra is to be honored
tomorrow: The stupa in the sky (Kern ch. 11)

lines: HOW MUCH DO YOU HAVE TO CARRY?
THE ONE WHO PASSES IT ALONG.
cards: A grandmother knows one proverb and says it at exactly the right moment, every time. Is she a teacher? How much of a teaching do you have to carry before you count as carrying it?
The whole book? A degree? A robe and a title?

Chapter ten of the Lotus Sutra answers, and its answer is smaller than the question. The Buddha turns to a bodhisattva named Bhaishajyaraja, the Medicine King, and talks about the figure the chapter is named for.
Not a great disciple, not a Buddha. Just someone who passes the words along.

teach.h: EVEN ONE VERSE, EVEN ONE MOMENT.
teach.b: First, the size of it. Whoever hears even a single verse of this sutra, the Buddha says, and is glad of it for one moment, he foretells their awakening.
Whoever keeps it, reads it, explains it or copies it, even one verse, and honors the book with flowers and incense, is to be honored as if they were the Tathagata himself.
Second, the messenger. Whoever explains this teaching to even one person, even quietly, in private, is a messenger the Tathagata has sent. One listener is enough.

teach.h: DIGGING FOR WATER IN DRY GROUND.
teach.b: A man in dry country digs for water. The sand comes up dry, and he keeps digging. Then the earth turns damp, then muddy, and he knows water is close.
Hearing this teaching, the Buddha says, is that damp earth: a sign that awakening is near. Fourth, how to do it.

teach.h: A ROOM, A ROBE, A SEAT.
teach.b: The chapter gives the preacher a room, a robe and a seat. The room is compassion for all beings. The robe is patience, gentleness under pressure.
The seat is seeing that all things are empty. Enter the room, put on the robe, sit on the seat, and then speak. So the preacher isn't the loudest voice.
It's anyone who carries one verse, kindly and patiently, to one other person. The bar is low. The honor is high.

how: In Mahayana communities that treasure the Lotus Sutra, people keep, recite, copy and explain the sutra, and the one who teaches it is honored; chapter ten is where the sutra itself praises that work.

o: a monk trained to give long sermons to big crowds
a scholar who has memorized the entire sutra
anyone who carries even one verse to one other person

games.q: even one verse: tap the pairs.
p: water is close; awakening is near

s: the chapter honors only those who know the whole sutra
even one verse, heard with gladness for one moment, is enough for the Buddha to foretell awakening.
explaining it to a single person makes you the Tathagata's messenger
even one person, even in private, says the chapter.
the preacher is told to speak first and find patience later
the chapter puts the room, robe and seat first: compassion, patience, emptiness. then speak.

games.q: you're digging for water in dry country. you've dug a while, and the sand is still dry. what do you do?
o: give up: there's no water here.
keep digging until the earth turns damp.
start a new hole somewhere else.
games.why: the digger keeps going. damp earth, then mud: he knows water is near. the Buddha says hearing this teaching is that damp earth.

practice: Bring to mind someone who handed you even one thing you still use: a line from a book, how to fold a shirt, how to apologize, what to do with your hands when you're scared. See their face and remember the moment they said it.
Then, in whatever way feels natural, bow to them inwardly, and rest there with the breath.

wordCard.voice: The preacher. In chapter ten, anyone who keeps or explains even one verse, even to one person, honored as a messenger of the Tathagata. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: one who recites or preaches the dharma, the 'preacher' of chapter ten.

carryVoice: Your line: even one verse. A grandmother's one proverb counts. Back tomorrow, same hill.
